AI Steering Committee.current_status: The AI Steering Committee has presented its comprehensive work, including a position statement, student handbook wording, and staff training on 'Magic School AI', with future plans for student AI education and a 'traffic light' protocol for assignments.
AI Steering Committee.overview:
On July 14, 2025, the Director of Technology, Andy Wallace, presented the AI Steering Committee's completed work. This included a position statement, specific wording for the student handbook regarding AI, and details on staff training for the approved 'Magic School AI' tool. Looking ahead, the committee outlined plans for integrating student AI education across all grade levels and implementing a 'traffic light' protocol to guide AI usage in student assignments. Superintendent Matheney, in his final report on the same date, also acknowledged the transformative impact of AI on education and society.

Prior to this, on July 8, 2024, the AI Steering Committee presented its initial findings. At that time, they recommended the adoption of 'Magic School AI' specifically for teachers and proposed a phased approach to AI competency training for both staff and students. The committee underscored the importance of ethical AI use and its integration into the curriculum, indicating that ongoing work was planned. The formation of this committee was initially announced by Superintendent Matheny on March 11, 2024, after he attended the National Conference on Education and recognized the accelerating impact of artificial intelligence on schools.

Superintendent Matheney, in his final report on the same date, highlighted AI's transformative impact. Earlier, on July 8, 2024, the AI Steering Committee recommended 'Magic School AI' for teachers and a phased approach to AI competency training, emphasizing ethical use. The committee itself was formed by Superintendent Matheny on March 11, 2024, following his attendance at a national conference where he noted AI's accelerating impact.

There is a recognized need for increased local and state support to ensure its long-term stability.
Adult Education.overview:
On December 9, 2024, Director Erin Krivicky provided an update on the Adult Education program, emphasizing its financial structure. She highlighted a significant dependence on grants for funding and articulated a clear need for greater local and state financial support to ensure the program's stability. Krivicky detailed the program's offerings, including ESOL and High Set, and introduced a new Integrated Education and Training (IET) program specifically tailored for the hospitality sector, underscoring the program's growth and future potential.

This funding challenge was previously noted on March 25, 2024, when the Adult Education department presented its budget and priorities. During that meeting, the department specifically highlighted its exponential growth, a trend that continues, and reiterated its reliance on unstable grant funding as a primary concern.

perspectives.Administration: Directors, including Erin Krivicky, consistently emphasize the Adult Education program's significant growth and future potential, particularly with new initiatives like the hospitality-focused IET program. They highlight the critical challenge of the program's heavy reliance on unstable grant funding and recommend the necessity of increased local and state financial support to ensure its long-term stability and continued expansion.

Cell Phone Policy.current_status: The board has unanimously approved the first reading of an amended Cell Phone Policy (JICI) that will prohibit cell phone use during the school day. Procedures for this new policy are to be developed with community engagement.
Cell Phone Policy.overview:
On June 8, 2026, the board unanimously approved the first reading of an amended Cell Phone Policy (JICI). This new policy is set to prohibit cell phone use during the school day, marking a significant shift from previous approaches. Discussions at this meeting highlighted the importance of community engagement in developing the specific procedures for implementing this policy.

This recent decision follows earlier discussions regarding cell phone use. On August 18, 2025, Student Representative Angela Kabisa informed the board about a slight shift in the high school's existing cell phone policy, which then required phones to be silenced and stored during home base and workshops. This update prompted a board discussion on the distinction between policy and actual practice, indicating a growing concern that has now culminated in the proposed full prohibition.

Chronic Absenteeism.current_status: Chronic absenteeism has decreased to 18%, a significant reduction attributed to restorative practices and an improved school climate. The board has praised these positive outcomes.
Chronic Absenteeism.overview:
On January 27, 2025, the board received a presentation indicating a decrease in chronic absenteeism to 18%. This reduction, along with a dramatic decrease in out-of-school suspensions, was attributed to the successful implementation of restorative practices and an improved school climate. The board specifically lauded these achievements, recognizing the positive influence of Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS).

Prior to this, on December 9, 2024, Superintendent Metheny reported a 3% improvement in chronic student absenteeism. During the same meeting, Principal Beth Kellogg of Brown School outlined several effective strategies, including fostering strong relationships, celebrating consistent attendance, ensuring clear communication regarding illness, and providing individualized support to families to encourage regular school attendance.

Earlier, on January 22, 2024, it was noted that chronic absenteeism rates were declining from their peak levels in the 2021-2022 academic year. These rates were moving in a positive direction and remained below the state average. The report also highlighted that high school students and economically disadvantaged students continued to experience higher rates of chronic absenteeism, while out-of-school suspensions at both middle and high school levels were also on a downward trend.

Community School Model.current_status: The Community School Model, successfully implemented at South Portland Middle School, has been approved for district-wide expansion, beginning with the high school. This expansion aims to leverage state funding and community partnerships.
Community School Model.overview:
On February 9, 2026, the SPSD Board voted to approve the expansion of the successful Community School Model across the district, starting with the high school. This decision followed a presentation by Dr. Rebecca Stern and Liana Popkin, who detailed the model's positive impact on absenteeism, family engagement, and academic achievement at South Portland Middle School. The expansion is intended to leverage state funding and foster community partnerships.

This approval built upon earlier successes and advocacy. On October 15, 2024, the middle school principal and community school director presented on their Community School model, which was initially funded by an ARPA grant. They outlined its six key practices, including powerful family engagement, shared leadership, extended learning opportunities, and integrated systems of support. The presentation highlighted positive outcomes such as reduced chronic absenteeism and increased grant funding, leading them to advocate for district-wide expansion and sustainable funding for the program.

These concerns prompted the Board to send the policy back to committee for further refinement, ensuring these points were addressed before its final approval.

District Goals 2024-2025.current_status: The SPSD has formally introduced its 2024-2025 annual goals, structured around four pillars: Instructional Excellence, DEIB, Planning for an Inspiring Future, and Operational Effectiveness. These goals include reducing chronic absenteeism and auditing practices for subgroup differences.
District Goals 2024-2025.overview:
On September 9, 2024, the Superintendent formally introduced the district's annual goals for 2024-2025. These goals are organized under four distinct pillars: Instructional Excellence, Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, & Belonging (DEIB), Planning for an Inspiring Future, and Operational Effectiveness. Specific objectives highlighted include efforts to reduce chronic absenteeism, conduct audits to address subgroup differences, and engage in strategic planning.

This framework builds upon the "Pillars & Priorities" initially introduced by the Superintendent on August 19, 2024. At that earlier meeting, a new 'Planning' pillar was added, specifically designed to focus on strategic planning, school boundaries, and configurations. The district also unveiled its new theme, 'Together We Grow,' on August 19, 2024, which aims to emphasize belonging and continuous improvement across the district. The September 9th meeting refined these pillars into the current "Planning for an Inspiring Future" and detailed specific goals under each.

perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent has introduced the 2024-2025 district goals, structured around four pillars: Instructional Excellence, DEIB, Planning for an Inspiring Future, and Operational Effectiveness. This framework, including a new 'Planning' pillar and the 'Together We Grow' theme, was developed to guide strategic planning, address chronic absenteeism, and promote equity and continuous improvement.

DEI Coordinator.overview:
On March 24, 2025, initial budget proposals for cuts included reducing the DEI Director to a Coordinator. While the board reached consensus on other cuts, such as eliminating the Director of Mental and Behavioral Health and freezing administrative salary increases, the specific outcome for the proposed reduction of the DEI Director role was not explicitly stated as approved. Public comments at this meeting, including from staff and administrators, expressed frustration with the budget process and raised specific concerns about the potential reduction of the DEI director's role.

This discussion follows the appointment of HermenegildoPaulo as the new Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion on May 30, 2024. His hiring as a Director came after the resignation of the previous DEI Coordinator, MohammedAlbehadli, on February 12, 2024.

MohammedAlbehadli's resignation was due to a racist incident, and on February 12, 2024, the board expressed gratitude for his work and reaffirmed the district's commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion. The current proposal to potentially reduce the Director role to a Coordinator represents a significant re-evaluation of the position's scope and resources amidst budget constraints, contrasting with the district's earlier reaffirmation of commitment.

This discussion follows the Superintendent's emphasis on March 31, 2025, regarding the district's 'unfinished work' in Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, where he advocated for the continuation of the Director of DEI position, citing student survey data on disparities in feelings of fairness and learning outcomes among different racial groups.

Earlier, on January 27, 2025, Superintendent Atkinson Duina presented data highlighting a significant increase in students of color (37%) and multilingual learners (16%) since 2019, underscoring the district's commitment to DEI. Elementary School Closure.current_status: Kaler Elementary School is approved for closure at the end of the 2025-2026 school year, with a modified schedule approved for its relocation. The district is addressing student reassignments and providing childcare for affected families during the transition.
Elementary School Closure.overview:
On June 4, 2026, the board approved a modified schedule for Kaler Elementary, including an early release on June 15th and no school on June 16th, to facilitate the school's relocation. This decision came after a vote on the schedule was postponed on May 27, 2026, to allow for adequate parental notification and comment. The district committed to providing free childcare for those in need on June 16th. On May 27, 2026, after an initial tie vote and reconsideration, the board approved the Kaler attendance zone proposal, with the understanding that Kaler families would be prioritized in the waiver process and transportation ensured for those granted waivers.

The decision to close Kaler Elementary School was formally approved by the board on March 30, 2026, effective at the end of the 2025-2026 school year. This closure was driven by declining enrollment and the need to capture fixed building costs, with the building remaining under the South Portland School Department's control for potential leasing. The Superintendent's budget for FY27, presented on March 23, 2026, highlighted a 12% staff reduction and the closure of one elementary school as necessary steps for financial sustainability, with Kaler Elementary specifically recommended for closure to allow for future leasing and revenue generation.

Earlier in the process, on March 9, 2026, the administration had proposed closing Dyer Elementary School, a shift from a previous week's proposal to close Skillin Elementary. This change was based on Dyer's higher projected five-year facility repair costs, particularly for its roof. The board's approval of Kaler's closure on March 30, 2026, superseded these earlier considerations regarding Dyer or Skillin.

On May 27, 2026, board members expressed strong reservations regarding the proposed Kaler attendance zones, particularly concerning the splitting of neighborhoods and the burden on Kaler families, leading to an initial tie vote. However, after further discussion, the proposal was approved with conditions prioritizing Kaler families for waivers and ensuring transportation. On March 30, 2026, the Board raised questions about the budget, the financial impact of Kaler's closure, the reconfiguration process, and potential staff morale issues before voting to approve the closure of Kaler Elementary.

Enrollment.current_status: Declining student enrollment is a primary driver of the district's current financial crisis, necessitating significant budget cuts and a re-evaluation of staffing levels. The district is facing a substantial budget gap largely due to this trend and rising costs.
Enrollment.overview:
On March 23, 2026, the Finance Director explained that the current financial crisis stems from a misalignment between declining enrollment and static staffing levels, alongside the depletion of the fund balance. This situation necessitates new policies and continuous adjustments for long-term financial health. Earlier, on March 2, 2026, the Board Chair acknowledged community concerns regarding elementary school reconfiguration, clarifying that the district needs to cut approximately $7-8 million, driven by declining enrollment and increased staffing, to meet budget guidelines. On February 4, 2026, Dr. Johanna Prince highlighted declining student enrollment and rising staffing costs as significant financial challenges, projecting an 18.95% tax increase and a $7.2 million budget gap if current services are maintained.

Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina reported a slight decrease in student enrollment on October 6, 2025. Prior to this, on May 27, 2025, the Superintendent's report noted that student enrollment had leveled out but was anticipated to decrease slightly in the following year due to graduating seniors and a smaller incoming kindergarten class. On March 17, 2025, key data revealed a projected 10% student enrollment decline since 2022, reaching a 15-year low, which contrasted with increased staffing levels over a similar period, creating a structural imbalance that the budget aims to address.

On September 9, 2024, the Superintendent noted a significant 7% decline in overall student enrollment, which was projected to impact state subsidy for FY26. This concern was reiterated on May 13, 2024, when Superintendent Duina reported a significant decline in student enrollment impacting future state subsidies. On April 8, 2024, Superintendent Duina reported current enrollment at 2,902 students and expressed concern about potential state subsidy reductions in FY26 due to declining enrollment. Earlier, on January 8, 2024, enrollment stood at 2,933, showing stabilization after previous fluctuations, though a potential loss of students was anticipated due to changes in temporary housing.

Enrollment Demographics.current_status: The SPSD is facing declining overall student enrollment alongside increasing populations of multilingual learners and special education students, which is depleting the district's fund balance and projecting a tax increase.
Enrollment Demographics.overview:
On December 17, 2025, a presentation to the board highlighted the critical financial implications of the district's changing demographics. It noted a continued decline in student enrollment, a rise in multilingual learners and special education students, and the subsequent depletion of the district's fund balance. These factors are projected to necessitate a tax increase, even if spending remains flat.

These recent developments build upon earlier reports. On January 27, 2025, Superintendent Atkinson Duina presented data indicating a significant increase in students of color (37%) and multilingual learners (16%) since 2019. Elementary School Reconfiguration.overview:
On July 20, 2026, new Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina included elementary reconfiguration work in her initial report, and Assistant Superintendent Jo Prince led a workshop to gather input on priorities such as student stability, access, equity, and operational logistics. This follows the Board's decision on April 29, 2026, and April 13, 2026, to delay the full elementary school reconfiguration until the 2027-2028 school year, a modification from the initial plan. This delay was made to allow for more thorough planning, community input, and to build trust, despite the Board having previously approved the Primary and Intermediate Model (Option A) for implementation in the 2026-2027 school year on March 30, 2026. An Elementary Reconfiguration Steering Committee, updated on May 11, 2026, is now developing the implementation plan, and Assistant Superintendent Jo Prince received additional compensation on June 8, 2026, for her extensive work on this and other initiatives.

The discussion around elementary school reconfiguration gained significant momentum from October 15, 2024, when the Superintendent reported declining enrollment and demographic disparities, leading to calls for addressing educational equity. By December 17, 2025, reconfiguration was identified as a key strategy for budget savings and structural changes, with an estimated $2M+ in savings noted on February 4, 2026. On February 9, 2026, the Board formally requested a proposal on reconfiguration's benefits and impact. The administration presented data on March 2, 2026, highlighting demographic disparities and proposing various scenarios, including the closure of Skillin Elementary (later shifted to Dyer Elementary on March 9, 2026, due to repair costs) and Kaler Elementary (recommended March 23, 2026). The Board ultimately approved Option A, the Primary and Intermediate Model, on March 30, 2026, which involved Pre-K-1 and 2-4 grade bands, aiming for equitable resource distribution.

Throughout early 2026, the reconfiguration process faced considerable challenges, including concerns about cost estimates, implementation plans, and community engagement, as raised on April 7, 2026, and April 2, 2026. The initial rapid timeline and proposed staff cuts, particularly in special education and related arts, drew strong opposition. The Board's decision to delay the full reconfiguration to Fall 2027 (announced April 13, 2026) was a direct response to extensive community feedback and a recognized need for a more thoughtful process. The FY27 Superintendent’s Budget, which included elements related to reconfiguration, was adopted by the board on April 7, 2026, despite some reservations.

FY27 Budget.overview:
On April 29, 2026, the board unanimously approved the various line items of the FY27 budget, including regular instruction, special education, student support, administration, transportation, facilities, and debt service. The overall budget was approved with a 6% tax impact, aligning with City Council guidance. This approval followed Finance Director Abigail Ketchen's presentation emphasizing financial stability and confirming the City Council's commitment to cover up to $2 million of the current year's deficit. Assistant Superintendent Dr. Johanna Prince detailed the final personnel changes, including the restoration of four SPTA positions, two special education ed techs, and one custodial position, made possible by insurance savings and one-time funding. On May 11, 2026, the Finance Committee reported a reduced deficit range for FY26-27 and ongoing efforts to implement payroll encumbrances for more accurate projections, alongside an update on the FY25 audit to improve internal processes.

Earlier, on April 7, 2026, the board had voted 4-2 to adopt the FY27 Superintendent’s Budget, advancing it to the City Council, despite some members expressing reservations about cuts and the reconfiguration timeline. This decision came after the Assistant Superintendent presented an update on a significant $655,000 reduction in the projected health insurance increase, which allowed for the proposed reinstatement of two elementary classroom teaching positions, two special education ed techs, and an SPTA related arts teacher. On April 2, 2026, Finance Director Abigail Ketchen presented the budget, highlighting past deficits and the need for realistic cost projections, while union representatives announced newly identified state funding. The board deferred a decision on adopting the budget then, opting to meet with the City Council for budgeting guidance. On April 13, 2026, the Board formally requested the City Council to offset $360,000 in costs for shared municipal services and requested a 1% tax increase to specifically seed the district's contingency fund.

The budget development process began with significant financial challenges. On December 17, 2025, Assistant Superintendent Johanna Prince outlined a projected tax increase even with flat spending due to declining enrollment and depleted fund balance, presenting options ranging from a 3.1% to a 22% tax increase. The board provided guidance to target a tax increase around 6.5%. On February 4, 2026, Dr. Prince projected an 18.95% tax increase if current services were maintained, leading to a $7.2 million budget gap against a 6% target, proposing strategies like elementary school reconfiguration, middle/high school schedule review, and operational efficiencies. On March 9, 2026, the administration proposed eliminating 78 positions, including 42 teachers, to meet a 6% tax increase cap. On March 23, 2026, the Superintendent's budget was presented, highlighting a 12% staff reduction and the closure of one elementary school. However, on March 30, 2026, the proposed FY27 Superintendent's Budget failed to pass, with a majority of board members voting against it due to concerns over specific cuts to student-facing positions and the desire for further discussion with the City Council regarding fund balance and potential additional revenue. This led to an additional meeting being scheduled to continue discussions and address community engagement.

On January 13, 2025, several policies were approved for first read or rescinded due to duplication, aiming to align with current regulations. This continued on May 13, 2024, with the rescission of outdated or redundant personnel policies. Key approvals included superintendent's job description updates (May 27, 2025), copyright compliance and field trip policies (March 10, 2025), and the Student Code of Conduct (JIC), Job Descriptions (GAB), School Board Legal Status (BB), and Board Member Conflict of Interest (BCB) on February 24, 2025. August 19, 2024, saw the approval of eighteen policies after a second reading, covering various operational aspects. The board also approved policies related to tobacco-free schools, physical restraint, and employee resignation on January 8, 2024, alongside rescinding other outdated policies. A new policy requiring the board to review and approve attendance zones every three years was also decided on May 13, 2024.

The decision was made to return to traditional snow days, meaning any missed instructional days due to weather closures will now be appended to the end of the school year. This move explicitly discontinues the use of remote learning days for snow days, a policy that had been in place previously. The primary rationale cited for this reversal was concerns regarding the effectiveness of remote learning, particularly for younger students.

Despite these strengths, the survey also highlighted critical areas for improvement. Specifically, school safety and students' sense of belonging, particularly among older students, were identified as needing attention. In response to these findings, ongoing efforts are underway, including the implementation of secure entry systems and the installation of safety film, to enhance the school environment.

South Portland High School Performance.current_status: South Portland High School is demonstrating positive trends in student attendance, significantly reduced out-of-school suspensions, and academic growth, including improved SAT scores and the piloting of new assessments. These improvements build on prior successes in reducing chronic absenteeism, course failure rates, and enhancing student well-being.
South Portland High School Performance.overview:
On May 27, 2025, the South Portland High School Principal presented a report highlighting several positive developments. The school observed favorable trends in student attendance, a notable decrease in out-of-school suspensions attributed to the implementation of PBIS (Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports), and academic progress evidenced by improved SAT scores. Additionally, the school is piloting NWEA pre/post assessments in mathematics to further gauge student learning.

These recent gains follow earlier positive reports. On July 8, 2024, South Portland High School reported a 6.8% decrease in chronic absenteeism, bringing the rate down from 42.3% to 35.5%. The school also achieved a substantial 66% reduction in out-of-school suspensions and saw course failure rates drop to 4.4%, indicating improved student engagement and academic outcomes.

Further back, on March 18, 2024, the school had already shown significant improvements in student well-being and academic pathways. Data from that meeting revealed a 4% increase in students' sense of belonging, a 41% reduction in bullying incidents, and an 11% increase in students feeling supported by their teachers. Suspension rates also saw considerable decreases, with in-school suspensions down by 34% and out-of-school suspensions by 63%. Concurrently, there was increased participation in Extended Learning Opportunities (ELOs) and dual/concurrent enrollment courses.

perspectives.Administration: The SPHS Principal and South Portland High School administration have consistently reported positive data trends across various metrics, including student attendance, chronic absenteeism, suspension rates (both in-school and out-of-school), academic performance (SAT scores, course failure rates), student well-being (sense of belonging, bullying incidents, teacher support), and participation in advanced learning opportunities (ELOs, dual/concurrent enrollment).

Student Achievement Data.overview:
On January 27, 2025, NWEA data presented to the board indicated consistent percentages of students requiring support in reading and math, prompting a continued focus on literacy initiatives. Additionally, post-secondary plans showed a significant increase in students attending two-year colleges, largely attributed to free tuition, which was viewed as a positive trend for college-bound students.

Previously, on January 22, 2024, student learning data from NWEA MAP assessments revealed that approximately half of students met grade-level benchmarks and about 40% met projected growth targets in math and reading. During this meeting, SAT scores were noted to be below state and national averages, which led to discussions about the necessity for focused instruction and early literacy initiatives.

Student Equity.overview: On March 28, 2024, the board raised concerns regarding equitable access to school events and sports for economically disadvantaged students and families. Special Education.overview:

Staff Reductions.current_status: The SPSD has recently restored several staff positions, including SPTA, special education ed techs, and custodial roles, for the FY2027 budget. These restorations were made possible by insurance savings and one-time funding, with special education positions further stabilized by new CDS funding.
Staff Reductions.overview:
Most recently, on April 29, 2026, Assistant Superintendent Dr. Johanna Prince confirmed the final personnel changes for FY2027, which included the restoration of four SPTA positions, two special education ed techs, and one custodial position. These reinstatements, initially proposed on April 7, 2026, were funded by health insurance savings and one-time funds, with special education roles benefiting from new CDS funding, ensuring their stability. This marks a significant reversal from earlier proposals for widespread reductions.

Prior to these restorations, the district faced substantial proposed staff reductions. On March 23, 2026, the Superintendent's budget for FY27 outlined a 12% staff reduction and the elimination of 78 positions, including 42 teachers and 16 educational technicians, as detailed on March 9, 2026. However, the proposed FY27 Superintendent's Budget failed to pass on March 30, 2026, due to board concerns over specific cuts to student-facing positions. Finance Director Abigail Katchen highlighted on April 2, 2026, the need for realistic cost projections to avoid future personnel losses, while board members questioned the rationale behind teacher cuts and their impact on students.

Looking back to the FY26 budget cycle, on March 10, 2025, significant staff reductions were proposed across various roles, including ESOL, SEL, and special education. By March 17, 2025, specific cuts like the Director of Curriculum, three SEL teachers, and two ESOL teachers were outlined. However, subsequent discussions led to some reinstatements; on March 31, 2025, Superintendent Metheny noted the restoration of a halftime STEM coordinator, one ESOL teacher, and a percussion ed tech. On March 24, 2025, the board also voted to reinstate the middle school Assistant Principal position, demonstrating a pattern of initial proposed cuts followed by public and board advocacy leading to some positions being restored or modified.

On March 30, 2026, a majority of board members voted against the proposed FY27 Superintendent's Budget, citing concerns over specific cuts to student-facing positions and the desire for further discussion with the City Council. Superintendent Search.current_status: The Board of Education has identified a preferred candidate for Superintendent and authorized the Chair to enter into negotiations. Further details are pending the completion of these discussions.
Superintendent Search.overview:
On May 11, 2026, the South Portland Board of Education announced that a preferred candidate for Superintendent had been identified, and the Chair was authorized to enter into negotiations. This development followed the announcement on April 29, 2026, of two finalists for the position, with a community meet-and-greet scheduled for May 6th. This update was shared amidst public comments expressing significant concern over the closed nature of the search process.

Board Chair Rosemarie DeAngelis also urged greater community participation in the ongoing superintendent search, noting low attendance at previous virtual sessions.

Discussions at that time highlighted the importance of a thorough search to find a long-term leader. Prior to this, on December 17, 2025, upcoming dates were announced for a public workshop on the superintendent search with Zeal and a community forum in January to gather input. On December 10, 2025, the board heard presentations from three superintendent search firms: Maine School Management Association (MSMA), NSEC, and Zeal Education Group. After discussing factors such as cost, board involvement, and community engagement, the board ultimately voted to select Zeal Education Group, contingent upon a positive reference check.

Superintendent Transition.current_status: An interim superintendent, Andy Wallace, has been appointed for a brief period in July 2026 to bridge the gap before the new superintendent officially begins. This follows a period with Interim Superintendent Dr. George Entwistle.
Superintendent Transition.overview:
On June 4, 2026, the board approved Andy Wallace as an interim superintendent for a two-week period in July, intended to bridge the gap before the new superintendent officially begins. Wallace agreed to serve without financial compensation, receiving four vacation days in exchange, and will consult with the incoming superintendent on any necessary decisions.

The transition process began on June 9, 2025, with the announcement of Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina's upcoming resignation and the initiation of a transition plan. Shortly after, on June 18, 2025, the board amended its agenda to include action on the search for an interim superintendent, emphasizing the importance of leadership consistency. They unanimously authorized the Maine School Management Association to assist with this search and also authorized the board chair and legal counsel to negotiate a separation agreement with Superintendent Matheney, contingent on the successful completion of the interim superintendent search.

On July 14, 2025, the board approved a separation agreement for Superintendent Matheney, effective August 8, 2025. Following this, George Entwistle was appointed as the interim superintendent for the 2025-2026 school year, with the board expressing confidence in his experience and leadership. Interim Superintendent Dr. George Entwistle reported on his first weeks on August 18, 2025, expressing positive impressions of staff professionalism and commitment, though he also announced several staff resignations and one retirement.
